chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mulla ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Mirdas, from Sa'dan ibn Muslim, from one of our companions, from Al-Harith ibn Hasirah, who said:

I passed an Ethiopian man who was supplying water in Medina, and behold, he had been cut. So I said to him, 'Who cut you?' He said, 'The best of people cut me. We were seized for theft, and we were eight persons. So we were taken to Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him), and we confessed to the theft. He said to us, 'Do you know that it is forbidden?' We said, 'Yes.' So he ordered that our fingers be cut from the palm, and the thumb was left.

Then he ordered that we be detained in a house where we were fed butter and honey until our hands healed. Then he ordered that we be brought out and clothed, and he dressed us well. Then he said to us, 'If you repent and amend your ways, that is better for you; Allah will attach your fingers to you in Paradise. And if you do not do so, Allah will attach your fingers to you in Hell.'
ai.seo_question: What did Imam Ali (peace be upon him) say to the thieves after amputating their fingers?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the nuanced application of hudud by Imam Ali (AS), emphasizing that amputation is not merely punitive but restorative, as evidenced by the thieves being fed butter and honey to heal their hands for future use. The Imam’s promise that Allah will 'unite their fingers with them' in the afterlife highlights a unique Shia theological perspective on the preservation of bodily integrity in Paradise for the repentant, linking physical healing to spiritual redemption. This narrative underscores the balance between justice and mercy, where the punishment serves as a catalyst for sincere tawbah rather than mere retribution.
